title: Manthara
hook: how a whisper works: not one big lie, but a picture of the future

segments.voice: Yesterday: Manthara on the rooftop, and Kaikeyi, glad, handing her a jewel. Did you notice your first feeling at someone's good news? Today, the jewel hits the floor, and the week closes. Day five hundred eighteen.

A conversation like this happens in offices and families every day. Someone takes you aside. They're not angry at you; they're worried for you. Haven't you noticed, they say, how things are going to go? And they paint you a picture of next year, and in the picture you're smaller, and someone else is laughing. Nothing they've said is quite a lie. But by the end, people you loved an hour ago look different. That's what happens in Kaikeyi's room tonight.
screen: `TAKEN ASIDE.` → `A PICTURE OF NEXT YEAR.` → `NOTHING QUITE A LIE.`

segments.voice: Manthara throws away the jewel and starts building the picture. Once Rama is king, she says, his son will be king after him, and Bharata will be cut out of the line forever. Worse, a king fears his brothers. Rama will send Bharata away, or have him killed. And you, she tells Kaikeyi, you were the king's favorite and you looked down on Kausalya. Now Kausalya will be the queen mother, and you'll stand in her hall like a servant. Kaikeyi pushes back at first. Rama is the eldest, she says. He's good, he's truthful, he treats me like his own mother. After him, Bharata may well reign. Valmiki lets her argue, which is worth noticing. She doesn't fall at the first push. But Manthara keeps going, and the picture gets sharper, and slowly Kaikeyi's face changes. By the end of the night she is asking, how? How do we stop this? Readers keep asking one question here: why did Manthara do it? Valmiki gives her loyalty to Kaikeyi and Bharata, and plenty of bitterness, and stops there. Later retellings add more. In some, including Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, the gods ask the goddess Sarasvati to turn Manthara's mind, so that Rama will go to the forest and, in time, defeat Ravana. That's a later answer, and a well-known one. Valmiki leaves the human version standing. And this closes a week that went from a sage's challenge on the road, to a glad assembly, a city lit for a coronation, a maid on a rooftop, and now a whisper in a queen's ear.
screen: `MANTHARA PAINTS THE FUTURE.` · `KAIKEYI PUSHES BACK.` · `HOW DO WE STOP THIS?` · `WHY DID MANTHARA DO IT?` · then, large: `A WEEK FROM A ROAD TO A WHISPER.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath slow. Think of a worry about the future you've been carrying, especially one that someone else handed you. Look at it as a picture rather than a fact. Notice who's in the picture, and how they're drawn. Then, with a breath out, imagine stepping back from it, so it's a little smaller and further off. You can come back to it later. For now, rest here. The bell holds the time.
Manthara. The maid who turns Kaikeyi's joy into fear, not with one big lie but with a picture of a future in which Bharata is lost.
Your line: how do we stop this. Today, when someone paints you a picture of how badly things will go, ask what's actually happened so far. Day five hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: In Ramlila and in homes where the Ramcharitmanas is read, the goddess Sarasvati turns Manthara's mind at the gods' request; readers of Valmiki often note that his telling leaves the motive human.

fork.setup: you're Kaikeyi. your oldest companion says Rama's crowning will ruin your son. what do you say first?
options: Rama is the eldest and good; Bharata may reign after him.
you're right; tell me what to do.
fork.reveal: Kaikeyi defends Rama first. only as Manthara keeps going does her face change, until she asks how to stop it.

original.note: Sanskrit kubjā: bent, hunchbacked. one of the names the text uses for Manthara.

trapdoor: what you thought: Manthara is the villain, and that's all.
what it means: she persuades by painting a future, and Kaikeyi resists before she gives way.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki leaves her motive human; the divine explanation, Sarasvati turning her mind, appears in later works such as the Ramcharitmanas.
recall: a king who became a sage
a crane or curlew, not a crow
